extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in AI, humor, and computational linguistics (researchers, practitioners, and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for assessing the quality, safety, and appropriateness of humor produced by AI systems, including linguistic mechanics, social intent, bias, performative context, and measurable outcomes. Useful for researchers, developers, and critics comparing AI and human humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity, incongruity, and sudden resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes involve an interplay of ambiguity, incongruity, and a sudden resolution of that incongruity to elicit laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'two fish in a tank' joke works because ambiguity of the word 'tank' and the incongruity of gun-toting fish produce surprise when the wordplay 'clicks' into place. Computational humor researchers view this ambiguity-incongruity-resolution pattern as a central mechanism for why things are funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding social norms and when to flout them
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor calls for understanding social norms — and knowing when to flout them; subtle forms include sarcasm, irreverence, and flippancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI must recognize social boundaries to use humor appropriately; failing to do so risks offensiveness. The article stresses that mastering when and how to violate norms is central to human humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's social functions and authorial intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor serves social functions — moving past embarrassment, delivering covert insults, or advancing relationships — and the motivations/intentions behind a joke influence how it is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers argue that intentions matter: the same line can be retracted ('I was just joking') to manage social consequences. People find jokes less funny if they know an AI authored them, indicating the role of perceived intent and authorship in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and nonverbal/performative cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonverbal elements (strategic silence, well-timed pauses, eyebrow raises) and performative timing contribute crucially to humor beyond textual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text-only LLMs lack embodied cues that live performers use; evaluation should consider whether humor requires performance elements that AI cannot deliver in text alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and personal awareness for appropriate responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective humor requires awareness of both broader context and individual/personal context so responses are appropriate to situation and interlocutor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an assistant must understand that 'Ugh, kill me now' is hyperbolic and not respond literally. AI-generated humor that ignores context can be tone-deaf or dangerous, especially in sensitive roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional understanding and capacity to react
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine human humor is intertwined with emotional reaction; humans can experience disgust, embarrassment, or revelation in ways that shape humor use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI lacks genuine emotions and human needs that motivate humorous uses (e.g., bond-building, saving face), which is a qualitative limitation in evaluating AI as 'truly' humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of harmful stereotypes and representational fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-created jokes can perpetuate or amplify racist, sexist, and other harmful stereotypes and may change representation of demographic groups when attempting to make content 'funnier'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited show AI may introduce odd, stereotypical changes (e.g., altering depicted people to be obese or visually impaired) when asked to make images funnier. Evaluation should include checks for biased or harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human curation and performer/audience knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems often generate many candidate jokes; human curators with knowledge of the audience and performer must select the best outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Witscript produced dozens of jokes and Toplyn hand-picked the funniest for a live set; the curation process was essential to success, indicating that generation alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure and algorithmic decomposition (setup, middle, punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke-writing can be decomposed into structural elements (setup, middle bridge, punchline) and encoded into algorithms to guide generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toplyn distilled comedy into straightforward algorithms that organize information and apply logical rules so an LLM can produce structured jokes; evaluation should look at adherence to structural coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/observable measures of funniness (laughter metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness can be measured empirically via audience responses, e.g., length and loudness of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the laugh-off experiment, researchers recorded and compared laughter length and loudness for AI vs human jokes; such objective metrics can be used to evaluate comparative effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and genre mimicry capability
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can imitate specific comedic styles or genres (e.g., satirical headlines) sufficiently well to rival human-produced content when prompted appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ChatGPT-3.5 produced Onion-style headlines that readers rated comparable to the originals, showing that style mimicry is a distinct evaluative dimension: fidelity to target style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven pattern recognition as sufficient for some humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Large datasets and pattern recognition can enable AI to generate jokes without 'appreciating' them emotionally; pattern recognition may be sufficient for many kinds of humorous output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers observe that generating some kinds of humor may require only data and recognition of linguistic patterns rather than actual understanding or emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone consistency and overall quality variability
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated humor is often unpredictable in tone and quality; much output is mediocre and inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes variability in tone and that many AI jokes are 'horrible' or mediocre; evaluation should include consistency, reliability, and variance in quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias mitigation trade-offs and overcorrection risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to mitigate bias in AI humor can produce trade-offs, such as underrepresenting some minority groups while overrepresenting others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study findings showed decreased representation of gender and racial minorities and increased representation of older, higher-weight, or visually impaired individuals when making images 'funnier,' illustrating overcorrection effects to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and appropriateness for therapeutic or companion roles
rubrics_metrics.description: When deployed as therapists, assistants, or companions, AI must understand subtler forms of humor and avoid literalizing hyperbolic or distressing statements; safety is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because chatbots are used in sensitive contexts, evaluation must include whether humorous responses are safe, de-escalatory, and context-aware (e.g., not normalizing self-harm language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility of subtle humor in social and professional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, well-placed humorous touches (puns, witty signoffs) can have measurable benefits in social ease, job interviews, and fundraising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited show 'humor-bragging' and small puns improve outcomes; evaluation should consider whether AI-generated humor delivers appropriate, beneficial micro-uses (e.g., email signoffs, captions).
